issues.legal_issue: Failure to file an undertaking required in connection with an extension of time to vacate does not by itself establish civil contempt when the person vacates within the original deadline.
material_facts: The order granted additional time to vacate subject to payment of outstanding dues and filing an undertaking within two weeks.
The respondent vacated the premises before the deadline in the order and did not file the undertaking.
issues.conclusion: The failure to file the undertaking was not a basis for initiating contempt action because the undertaking was required only if the respondent wished to avail of the additional time, which the respondent did not need.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Sections 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, civil contempt requires wilful disobedience. Ram Kishan v. Tarun Bajaj (2014) explains that the disobedience must be deliberate and established beyond reasonable doubt; a failure that does not amount to wilful disobedience does not justify contempt action.

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A court is considering an allegation of civil contempt for disobedience of its order.
predicates.undertaking_conditioned_on_extra_time: The order requires an undertaking only as a condition for using additional time to comply.
predicates.vacated_before_original_deadline: The person vacated the premises before the deadline that applied without the additional time.

issues.definition: If a civil contempt allegation concerns an undertaking required only to obtain extra time and the person vacates before the original deadline, the omission alone does not establish contempt.

issues.legal_issue: A failure to pay disputed dues does not amount to wilful disobedience in contempt proceedings when the order did not decide the liability and the person acted on a bona fide understanding of the order.
material_facts: The respondent disputed that any amount remained payable, relying on the parties’ arrangements and the petitioner’s alleged continued use of a trademark.
The High Court had left the parties to pursue the disputed accounts and liability in execution proceedings, and the order alleged to have been breached did not determine the amount payable.
The respondent maintained a bona fide understanding that no dues were outstanding.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no intentional violation or wilful disobedience on the dues allegation and left the parties to pursue their claims in execution proceedings or other proceedings permitted by law; it did not decide the underlying liability.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Sections 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, contempt requires wilful disobedience proved beyond reasonable doubt. Ram Kishan v. Tarun Bajaj (2014) holds that bona fide conduct and genuine interpretive uncertainty do not establish wilfulness, and that where two interpretations are possible and conduct is not contumacious, contempt is not maintainable. R.N. Dey v. Bhagyabati Pramanik (2000) holds that contempt should not be used instead of an available execution remedy. Jhareswar Prasad Paul v. Tarak Nath Ganguly (2002) holds that a contempt court cannot decide matters not determined by the order allegedly breached and should leave ambiguous or undecided matters to the appropriate court.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and dues_liability_not_decided_in_order and execution_forum_left_claim_open and bona_fide_understanding_no_dues

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A court is considering an allegation of civil contempt for disobedience of its order.
predicates.dues_liability_not_decided_in_order: The order said to have been breached did not determine whether dues were payable or their amount.
predicates.execution_forum_left_claim_open: A court left the parties to pursue their disputed payment claims in execution proceedings or another lawful proceeding.
predicates.bona_fide_understanding_no_dues: The person relied on a bona fide understanding that no dues were outstanding.

issues.definition: When an order leaves payment liability undecided, another forum is left to resolve it, and the person acts on a bona fide understanding that no dues are outstanding, the disputed non-payment does not establish wilful contempt and the liability remains for other proceedings.

issues.legal_issue: Alleged damage to property does not warrant contempt action when the evidence does not establish permanent damage or intentional disobedience and the dispute is factually complex.
material_facts: The allegation of damage relied on photographs showing debris at the premises.
The respondent produced photographs showing the condition of the premises when vacated and relied on its entitlement to remove certain fixtures.
The water park became functional within two to three months, and any minor repairs were not shown to be intentional disobedience.
issues.conclusion: The Court found that the damage allegation did not warrant contempt action and left the property-condition claim open to be pursued in execution proceedings or another proceeding permitted by law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Sections 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, contempt requires wilful disobedience proved beyond reasonable doubt. Ram Kishan v. Tarun Bajaj (2014) excludes negligent, inadvertent, or otherwise non-wilful conduct from contempt. R.N. Dey v. Bhagyabati Pramanik (2000) cautions against using contempt instead of an available remedy for enforcement or resolution of a disputed claim.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and property_damage_allegation and evidence_does_not_establish_permanent_damage and damage_dispute_is_factually_complex

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A court is considering an allegation of civil contempt for disobedience of its order.
predicates.property_damage_allegation: A person alleges that property was damaged while another person was vacating it.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_permanent_da: The evidence, including the condition of the property afterward, does not establish permanent damage to its structure.
predicates.damage_dispute_is_factually_complex: Resolving the property-condition claim requires determination of disputed facts beyond the contempt allegation.

issues.definition: When a civil contempt proceeding includes a factually complex property-damage allegation but the evidence does not establish permanent damage, the allegation does not warrant contempt and remains open for other proceedings.

issues.legal_issue: A court may retain part of a deposit to secure disputed claims pending their determination and permit withdrawal of the excess subject to safeguards.
material_facts: The respondent had deposited money in the contempt proceeding and sought to withdraw the excess over the amount it proposed should remain secured.
The Court relegated the parties to the executing court to pursue their competing claims arising from their agreements.

The Court directed that the amount it considered appropriate to retain, with accrued interest, be transferred to the executing court and allowed withdrawal of the excess subject to an undertaking to repay if directed and the provision of solvent security.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed transfer of the retained portion and accrued interest to the executing court, and permitted withdrawal of the excess subject to an undertaking to redeposit it if required and to furnishing solvent security.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion to secure the parties’ competing interests while leaving their underlying claims for determination by the executing court. No earlier case was cited for this specific deposit arrangement.

predicates.disputed_claims_relegated_to_execution: A court has left competing claims for determination in execution proceedings.
predicates.deposited_funds_available: Funds have been deposited with the court in connection with the dispute.
predicates.depositor_seeks_excess_withdrawal: The depositor asks to withdraw funds beyond the portion proposed to remain secured.

issues.definition: When disputed claims are left for execution, funds are held by the court, and the depositor seeks the excess, the excess may be withdrawn subject to a repayment undertaking and solvent security.
